title: A-Level Results Are In! Here's What's Different This Year
summary:
Imagine waiting all summer for one envelope or email that could change your future. That's what happened for thousands of UK teens on Thursday, August 13, 2026, when A-level, T-level, and BTec results came out. This year, everyone is watching what teens decide to do next.

Here's a big number: a record number of 18-year-olds in the UK have been accepted into university, according to UCAS (the Universities and Colleges Admissions Service). More than ever got into their first choice. But here's the twist: because there are more 18-year-olds than before, the actual percentage who got their first choice fell from 82% to 79%. So it's a record, but also a bit of a letdown for some.

Top grades are still lower than in 2020 and 2021, when exams were cancelled and teachers gave grades instead. Since then, grades have been brought back down. In England, grading returned to pre-pandemic levels in 2023, and Wales and Northern Ireland followed in 2024. But the share of top grades (A* and A) has been creeping up a little since 2023.

Universities are really keen to get students in the door. Why? Money. Every filled seat means tuition fee funding. But many universities are struggling financially. Four in 10 universities in England are expected to report a financial deficit in 2025-26. That's because tuition fees for UK students have been frozen for a long time, and fewer international students are coming.

Teens are also worried about money. Many are using Clearing (a system to find courses with open spots) to find courses closer to home to save cash. But even with worries about rising tuition fees and student loans, the percentage of UK 18-year-olds applying to university has stayed about the same. So the dream of a degree is still alive, even if it's getting more expensive.
why_it_matters: The story shows how competition and money affect who gets into university, which can shape the choices you make about school later.

background_read: UCAS (the Universities and Colleges Admissions Service) is the central system where UK students apply for university places.
In 2020 and 2021, COVID-19 stopped normal exams, so teachers awarded grades instead of students sitting tests.
England, Wales, and Northern Ireland have returned to pre-pandemic grading, but Scotland has its own exam system.
